title: No mocking, no nicknames
hook: don't mock others, they may be better than you, and don't insult with names (49:11)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Islah, the mending the verse gives to bystanders. Your line: repair with fairness, so the thing can hold.
screen: `REPAIR WITH FAIRNESS, SO THE THING CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: Maybe you had one: the nickname from middle school that started as a joke about your ears, your name, your accent, your weight, and followed you for years. Some people laugh about theirs now. Some still flinch when they hear it. The people who gave them out mostly forgot within a week. Surah Al-Hujurat spends a whole verse on this, and the reason it gives is not the one you'd expect.

Verse eleven, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they (are), nor let women (deride) women who may be better than they are; neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames." Three things are named. Mocking, sakhar: laughing at someone to make them small. Defaming, lamz: the little dig, the jab disguised as a joke. And insulting with nicknames, tanabuz bil-alqab: the label that sticks. Then the reason. Not that mocking is rude, but that the one you mock may be better than you. You can see a person's ears or accent. You can't see their standing with God. Mockery assumes a ranking the mocker has no access to. A report in Sunan Abi Dawud gives the setting. A man from the Banu Salamah said the verse came down about them. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina, many men had two or three names, and when he called someone by one of them, people would say: Messenger of God, that one makes him angry. So the verse was revealed. Notice: the Prophet himself didn't know which names stung. Nicknames aren't always cruel. Many Companions carried names they loved, like Abu Hurayrah, father of the little cat. The line the scholars draw is the verse's own: whether the name is one the person dislikes. A hadith in Sahih Muslim sums it up: it is evil enough for a person to look down on his brother.
screen: `MOCKING, DIGS, AND LABELS THAT STICK.` · `THEY MAY BE BETTER THAN YOU.` · `NAMES THAT MADE SOMEONE ANGRY.` · `ABU HURAYRAH LOVED HIS.`

segments.voice: Think of the names you use for people, out loud or in your head: a coworker, a sibling, a politician, a driver who cut you off, and find one that's really a small insult. Picture that person hearing it, and set it down in favor of their real name. If you were given a name that still stings, you can let yourself set that down too, and if you pray, you can pray for them.
No mocking. The rule of 49:11: no deriding, no digs, no hurtful nicknames, because the one you mock may be better than you. Today's word.
Your line: they may be better. Nobody sees the whole of anyone else. That's day five hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars count mocking and hurtful nicknames among the sins of the tongue; affectionate names a person welcomes, like Abu Hurayrah, are accepted, while names someone dislikes are avoided.

chat.says: It's just a nickname. Why would the Qur'an care about that?
options: It bans hurtful nicknames: the one you mock may be better than you.

chat.meaning: 49:11 forbids mocking, digs and names people dislike, because the one mocked may be better. Companions kept nicknames they loved.

sakhar.meaning: mocking, laughing at someone to make them small

Banu Salamah.meaning: a clan of Medina whose men had several names
